3.title: Knowing Christ: The Surpassing Worth and the Pressing Forward
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the letter’s most autobiographical passage and contains the most shattering personal testimony in Paul’s letters. He has been warned to write certain things before (v. 1: “to write the same things to you is no trouble to me”), and now he does so with increasing urgency: beware the dogs, the evildoers, the mutilators of the flesh — the Judaizers who are insisting on circumcision as the ground of standing with God. Paul’s counterargument is not theoretical but personal: he has everything the Judaizers are offering, and more. His Jewish credentials are impeccable. And he counts them all as loss — as refuse, as dung — compared to the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord.

The word “knowing” (gnōsis tou Christou) is not intellectual acquaintance but the knowing of deep personal relationship — the knowing of shared experience, of shared suffering, of being conformed to his death and participating in his resurrection. Paul wants to know Christ in his resurrection power and in the fellowship of his sufferings. He does not want the triumph without the cross, the exaltation without the humiliation, the glory without the pain. This is the anti-triumphalism that runs through all his letters: the Christ who was crucified before he was raised sets the pattern for Christian existence.

The chapter then turns to one of Paul’s most powerful metaphors: the runner pressing on toward the finish line. He has not yet arrived; he does not count himself as having obtained it. But he presses on, stretching forward to what lies ahead. The past — with all its achievements and all its failures — is left behind. The prize is ahead. And the warning at the chapter’s end about the enemies of the cross of Christ — whose god is their belly, whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things — sets the urgency of pressing forward in sharp relief: there is a road that leads elsewhere, and many travel it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Everything I Had, and What It Was Worth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns a corner — “finally” is a hinge, not a conclusion — with a command to rejoice in the Lord, and an unembarrassed note that he does not mind repeating himself, because repetition is a safe footing for them (v.1). Then the tone hardens. Three times: look out. The people pressing circumcision on Gentile believers are called dogs, evildoers, and mutilators — katatome, a hacking, against peritome, circumcision (v.2). For the true circumcision is the church: those who worship by the Spirit, glory in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh (v.3).

Then Paul plays his hand, so that nobody can dismiss him as a man rejecting what he never had (v.4). Four inherited privileges — circumcised the eighth day, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews — and then the achievements: a Pharisee as to the law (v.5), a persecutor of the church as to zeal, and blameless as to the law’s righteousness (v.6).

And the whole column is moved to the other side of the ledger. Whatever was gain he counted loss for Christ’s sake (v.7); more than that, he counts everything loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord, and reckons it all skybala — refuse, what is thrown to the dogs — in order to gain Christ (v.8). His aim is to be found in him, not with a righteousness of his own from the law but the righteousness from God that depends on faith (v.9); to know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being shaped to the pattern of his death (v.10); and so by any means to attain the resurrection of the dead (v.11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification: A Righteousness From Outside

Verse 9 is among the clearest statements of justification in the New Testament, and its decisive word is own. Paul does not say his law-righteousness was insufficient, or that he needed more of it; he has just called himself blameless. He says he does not want it — it is the wrong kind of thing. A righteousness of one’s own can produce only two outcomes, and both are fatal: if you believe you have achieved it, it makes a Pharisee, and Paul has shown you what that produced in him; if you know you have not, it crushes you.

Against it stands a righteousness that comes through faith and from God — faith being the channel and not the achievement, the beggar’s open hand rather than the coin. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: Christ’s record credited to those who are in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness, alien not because it is strange but because it comes from outside — which is exactly its comfort. A standing that rests on his record is the same on your worst day as on your best, and will be the same on the day you are found in him.

Verse 11 should not be read as doubt. The man who has written that to die is gain and that departing is far better is not privately unsure whether he will be raised. “By any means possible” is openness about the route, not uncertainty about the destination.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the Philippians a supplement — faith plus circumcision, grace plus performance. Paul’s answer is autobiographical and devastating: I held the complete set, more of it than any of you, and beside Christ it went out with the kitchen refuse. Note that this is not a man who found his old life worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was real gain; he met something beside which it could not hold its value. Carry a lamp outdoors at noon and you would set it down and forget it, and nothing has happened to the lamp.

Now: “Flesh” in verse 3 is wider than circumcision. It means anything about you that could be offered as a reason God should accept you — family, record, discipline, usefulness, the fact that you have never done anything really disgraceful. The question is not whether you have such things; Paul had an impressive set. It is whether any weight rests on them, and the honest way to find out is to notice what happens inside you when one is taken away. Paul is not asking whether you would say Christ is worth more than your reputation. He is asking what actually happened the last time your reputation was threatened.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Finally” is a word that has misled generations of readers, and preachers have made jokes about it. It does not mean Paul is winding up — he has two chapters to go, and the sharpest passage in the letter is about to begin. The Greek phrase means something more like as for the rest, or and so. It is a hinge, not a conclusion.

“Rejoice in the Lord.” Notice first that it is an imperative. Paul is not observing that joy is pleasant or wishing it on them; he is commanding it, as he will again in 4:4. And that ought to stop us, because you cannot order someone to feel something. Tell a grieving man to be happy and you have only added a burden to his grief.

The answer is in the two words that follow the verb. The command is not “be cheerful”; it is “rejoice in the Lord” — and that names an object, not a mood. Paul is not telling them to generate a feeling out of nothing. He is telling them to look at someone, on the reasonable assumption that joy will follow the looking. What can be commanded is where you direct your attention.

And see what the object is not. Not his circumstances, which amount to a cell and a pending capital charge. Not the health of the church, which has a quarrel in it he will have to name. Not the absence of enemies, since he is about to spend seventeen verses on enemies. Christian joy is not the conclusion you reach after surveying your situation; it is the place you stand while you survey it. Which is why a man in prison can command it of a church in comfort without absurdity.

Then a curious sentence: “To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.” What same things? He may mean the call to rejoice, which he does keep repeating. He may mean the warning that follows, which he says in verse 18 he has often told them before. Either way, the principle is worth having, because it cuts against a real instinct in teachers and preachers: the fear of being boring.

Paul is not embarrassed to repeat himself. He gives two reasons and they are beautifully matched. It costs him nothing — “no trouble to me” — and it protects them: the word is asphales, the term for something secure, unlikely to slip; it is used of a ship’s safe anchorage and of a firm foothold. Repetition is not the teacher’s failure of imagination. It is the hand-rail on the stair.

Which is worth saying to anyone who has ever sat through a sermon on a text they already knew and felt vaguely cheated. The things a Christian most needs to hear are almost never new. They are the same handful of truths, driven in again, because we leak. Paul knew that about the Philippians and he knows it about us, and he refuses to be too sophisticated to say a thing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone changes without warning. Three times in one verse: blepete — look out, watch, keep your eye on. And three names for the same people, each one calculated to sting.

“The dogs.” In the ancient world dogs were not pets; they were the scavengers that worked the rubbish heaps outside the town, unclean and half-wild. And “dog” was the standard Jewish insult for a Gentile — the outsider, ceremonially filthy, outside the covenant. Paul picks the word up and turns it round. The people insisting that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong are themselves the dogs: they are the ones outside, scavenging at the edge of a covenant they have not understood.

“Those who mutilate the flesh.” Here is a pun that does not survive into English. Circumcision is peritome — a cutting around. Paul calls what they practise katatome — a cutting down, a hacking; the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the pagan gashing that the law forbade (Lev 21:5; 1 Kgs 18:28). His point is not that circumcision was never anything. It is that a sign severed from the thing it signified is no longer a sign. Take away the covenant reality and what remains is not a sacrament. It is surgery.

Then the counter-claim, and it is breathtaking: “we are the circumcision.” Not “we are the true spiritual equivalent of it” — we are it. A congregation of Macedonian Gentiles, most of them uncircumcised, is told they are the covenant people, and the men pressing the knife are not. This is what the prophets had said all along: circumcise the foreskin of your heart (Deut 10:16; Jer 4:4), for the real Jew is one inwardly (Rom 2:28–29).

And Paul defines it by three marks, which together make a fair test of any church or any soul. First, “who worship by the Spirit of God” — not by machinery, ritual, or technique, but by the Spirit himself. Second, “and glory in Christ Jesus” — the boast has moved outside the self altogether. Third, “and put no confidence in the flesh.”

That third mark is the one to sit with, because “flesh” here is broader than circumcision. It means everything about you that could be offered as a reason God should accept you: your family, your record, your discipline, your usefulness, the fact that you have never done anything really disgraceful. The question is not whether you have such things. Paul is about to list an impressive set of his own. The question is whether any weight is resting on them — and the honest way to find out is to notice what happens inside you when one of them is taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now does something risky. Having said the Christian puts no confidence in the flesh, he immediately says: “though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also.” He will not let anyone dismiss him as a man rejecting what he never had. If this is a competition, he says, I can win it — and then he lists his hand.

The list falls cleanly into two halves. The first four are things done to him before he could have any say. “Circumcised on the eighth day” — not a proselyte circumcised as an adult, not an Ishmaelite circumcised at thirteen, but exactly on the day the law required. “Of the people of Israel” — the covenant nation. “Of the tribe of Benjamin” — and that is a real boast: Benjamin gave Israel her first king, whose name Paul carried; Benjamin alone stayed with Judah when the kingdom tore in two; and Jerusalem itself sat in Benjamin’s territory. “A Hebrew of Hebrews” — a Diaspora family that had kept the language and the ways when it would have been easier to let them go.

Then three things he achieved himself. “As to the law, a Pharisee” — not the sneering caricature but the most rigorous and most respected school in Judaism, men who had given their lives to obeying God in the detail. “As to zeal, a persecutor of the church” — and note that he offers this as a credential. In the tradition of Phinehas and the Maccabees, zeal that acted was the proof of a serious man. Paul is telling them, without flinching, that on the old accounting his worst act was his best qualification.

“As to righteousness under the law, blameless.” This one stops the modern reader, because we expect the man of Romans 7 to say the opposite. But he is not claiming sinlessness. He is talking about observable, public, external compliance — the record any neighbour in Tarsus or Jerusalem could inspect. On that measure there was nothing to point at. Which is precisely the horror of his position, and he intends us to feel it: this man kept the rules impeccably and was, at the same time, the chief enemy of the Son of God. Blamelessness had not made him good. It had made him dangerous.

And that is the argument. The Judaizers are offering the Philippians a package. Paul says: I had the complete set — birth, pedigree, sect, zeal, and an unblemished record — more of it than any of you. So when I tell you what it is worth, understand that I am not making a virtue of what I lacked.

verseByVerse.quote: But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the ledger, and Paul keeps it in the vocabulary of the counting-house. He has already used the verb twice in chapter 2 — Christ did not count equality with God something to exploit; you are to count others more significant. Here he applies the same reckoning to his own accumulated assets, and moves every one of them across the page.

Watch the escalation, because it happens in three stages. First: “whatever gain I had, I counted as loss” — past tense, the moment on the Damascus road when the books were rewritten. Second: “indeed, I count everything as loss” — present tense, and the category has widened from his religious credentials to everything. That first verdict was not a young convert’s enthusiasm; thirty years later he is still saying it, and saying it wider.

Third, and this is where the language turns violent: “I count them as rubbish.” Skybala is not a polite word, and “rubbish” is a translator’s kindness. It meant what was thrown out to the dogs — kitchen refuse, and, in its coarser use, excrement. Paul has just called his opponents dogs; now he says his own pedigree is what you throw to them. The man is not being decorous. He is trying to make a church feel the difference in value, and he chooses the strongest word available.

But do not misread the arithmetic. This is not a man who decided his old life was worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was genuinely valuable — the covenant, the law, the zeal, all of it real gain. What happened was that he met something beside which they could not hold their value. The phrase is “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.” Bring a lamp into a room at night and it is a genuine treasure; carry it outside at noon and you would put it down and forget it. Nothing has happened to the lamp.

And notice the two words that make the sentence personal: “my Lord.” Paul is not describing a doctrine. In the whole of his letters he says “my Lord” almost nowhere else. Whatever else the Damascus road did, it left this man with a person he could call his own, and everything he had spent forty years accumulating went out with the kitchen scraps to make room for him.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Paul is not asking whether you would say Christ is worth more than your career, your family name, your reputation for soundness. Everyone in church says that. He is asking what actually happened the last time one of them was threatened — and whether the loss felt like the loss of a lamp at noon, or like the end of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the doctrinal centre of the letter and one of the clearest statements of justification in the New Testament. Every phrase is load-bearing.

“And be found in him.” Found by whom, and when? On the day of Christ, the day this letter keeps returning to (1:6, 10; 2:16). Paul is imagining the final inspection — and his entire strategy for it is to be discovered inside someone else. Not standing beside Christ with his own record in his hand. In him.

“Not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law.” The crucial word is own. Paul is not saying his law-righteousness was inadequate, or that he had less of it than he needed. He has just told us he was blameless. He is saying he does not want it. It is the wrong kind of thing altogether — not a small coin but a forged one, and the trouble with a forged coin is not that it is small.

Why the wrong kind? Because a righteousness of your own can only ever produce one of two results, and both are fatal. If you think you have achieved it, it makes you a Pharisee — and Paul has just shown you what that produced in him. If you know you have not, it crushes you. There is no third outcome. The whole system can generate pride or despair and nothing else.

Against it: “that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith.” Note the two prepositions doing the work. It comes through faith — faith is the channel, not the achievement; and it is from God — his own righteousness, given. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: a righteousness that is not produced in me but credited to me, Christ’s record entered in my account because I am in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness — alien not because it is strange but because it comes from outside, and that is precisely its comfort.

And faith itself contributes nothing to the transaction; it is simply the empty hand. A beggar’s open palm is not what buys the bread. Which is why assurance is possible at all. If my standing rested on a righteousness of my own, every bad week would move the ground under me. Because it rests on his, my standing on my worst day is exactly what it was on my best — and it will be the same on the day I am found in him.

verseByVerse.quote: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“That I may know him.” Everything in the passage has been building to this, and the smallness of the object is the point. Not that I may know about him; not even that I may know his benefits. Him.

The verb matters. Greek has a word for knowing facts, and this is not primarily it. This is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when Adam knew his wife, and when God says of Israel “you only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). It is knowledge by acquaintance and covenant, the knowing that happens between persons. And here is the striking thing: the man writing has been an apostle for something like thirty years, has seen the risen Christ, has been caught up to the third heaven — and he writes as though he were still at the beginning. Nobody in the New Testament knew Christ better, and nobody wanted to know him more.

Then Paul unfolds what this knowing involves, and he yokes two things most of us would prefer to separate: “the power of his resurrection, and… his sufferings.” They are held under one article in the Greek, as a single object. Not two experiences to be chosen between. One thing with two faces.

Note the order, which is not chronological. In Christ’s own life the suffering came first and the resurrection after; Paul reverses it. That is because he is describing the Christian’s experience rather than Christ’s history: you meet the risen Lord first, and it is his resurrection power that then makes it possible to walk into suffering at all. Nobody shares Christ’s sufferings on his own steam.

“Becoming like him in his death” is one word, symmorphizomenos — and there is morphe again, the word from 2:6–7, the form of God and the form of a servant. The hymn is not left behind in chapter 2; it is being pressed into Paul. He is being shaped into the same form his Lord took — the form of the one who poured himself out. It is the present tense, continuous: a thing being done to him while he writes, in a cell, awaiting a verdict.

Which is worth naming plainly, because this verse is often quoted with the second half left off. Christians ask for resurrection power constantly and rarely for fellowship in his sufferings. Paul asks for one thing containing both, and he does not seem to regard it as the price of the power. He regards it as part of the prize — because it is the way you come to know a person, and the person he wants to know went to a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“That by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.” The sentence sounds uncertain, and it has troubled readers who have just been told in 1:6 that God finishes what he starts. Is Paul hedging about whether he will be raised?

He is not, and the letter itself settles it. This is the man who has said that to die is gain, that departing is far better, that he will be with Christ. Two verses ahead he will say Christ has already made him his own. Nobody who writes those sentences is privately unsure whether he is saved.

What the phrase expresses is not doubt about the outcome but openness about the route. “By any means possible” means: whatever it takes, whatever road it goes by, however God chooses to bring me there. Paul does not know whether he reaches the resurrection through a Roman sword or through years more of labour and an old man’s bed. He is not attached to the road. He is attached to the destination, and he is saying he will accept any terms.

There is also a note of reverent seriousness in it that we should not sand away. A Christian can be certain of the end and still refuse to be casual about the journey. The New Testament holds both without embarrassment: God will keep you, and you must press on. The same Paul who wrote “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” wrote “I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Cor 9:27). The certainty never produces a shrug.

There is a pastoral use for this, too. Christians sometimes fear that any uncertainty in them proves their faith is counterfeit. Paul’s sentence is a useful corrective. A man utterly sure of his destination can still write a cautious-sounding line about the road, because the caution is not about God’s faithfulness but about his own ignorance of what the next year holds. Not knowing what is coming is not the same as doubting who is waiting.

And notice which resurrection he means. Not the general raising of all the dead, which requires no striving from anyone; the wicked are raised too (John 5:28–29). Paul means the resurrection of the righteous, the one that is glory — the thing he will describe in verse 21, this humiliated body remade like Christ’s. That is what he is running for. He is not anxious about arriving. He is simply willing to get there any way God likes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Not Arrived, and Still Running
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having written the loftiest sentences in the letter, Paul immediately guards them: he has not obtained it and is not already perfect, but presses on to make it his own — because Christ Jesus has already made him his own (v.12). He says it again, flatly, and then names his single occupation: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (v.13), pressing toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus (v.14).

Then a turn that is easy to miss. Let those who are mature think this way — using the very word he has just refused for himself — and if any of them think otherwise, God will reveal that to them too (v.15). Meanwhile, the floor: let us hold true to what we have already attained, and keep in step with it (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Sanctification Is Progress, Not Arrival

The Reformed tradition has always held that sanctification in this life is real but incomplete — the Westminster Confession speaks of it as imperfect in this life, with remnants of corruption abiding in every part. Verse 12 is the apostle’s own testimony to exactly that, and it is aimed at anyone claiming a settled plateau where striving is over.

The engine of the passage is the second half of verse 12: I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. The same verb both times — to seize, to lay hold of. Paul chases Christ because Christ has already caught him on the Damascus road, while he was travelling the other way with warrants in his bag. Get that order wrong and the Christian life is unbearable: running in order to be apprehended is exhausting and never finished. Running because you were apprehended is another thing altogether, and it is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him.

Verse 15 then supplies the paradox that defines maturity: the teleioi are precisely those who know they are not yet teleios. Anyone who believes he has finished has thereby proved he has not begun to think properly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some in the early church claimed a completed spiritual state, and Paul’s disclaimer is a direct correction of it. But note how he handles the difference in verse 15 — he does not repeat the argument louder or threaten. He hands them to God and expects God to do the persuading. That is patience, not indifference: he plainly thinks he is right and expects them to come round.

Now: Two applications. First, on disagreement. Paul gives no ground whatever on the gospel itself — there the language is dogs and mutilators — and is patient about the outworking of the pressing-on life, where sincere Christians differ. Knowing which sort of question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom; treat every disagreement as first-order and you will shred a congregation, treat none as first-order and you will lose the gospel. Second, on the past. Biblical forgetting is not amnesia — Paul remembers his perfectly well and has just listed it. It means refusing to let it govern, and it cuts both ways: the runner must forget his failures, which the guilty Christian needs to hear, and his successes, which is harder and far less often preached.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having written some of the loftiest sentences in Scripture, Paul immediately puts a guard on them: “Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect.” It is one of the most important disclaimers in the New Testament. There were people in the first century, as there have been in every century since, who taught that a Christian could arrive — reach a settled plateau where the striving was over. Paul, of all people entitled to claim it, refuses.

Then the sentence that turns the whole passage: “but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.” Same verb both times — to seize, to lay hold of, to catch. Paul is chasing Christ because Christ has already caught him. That is the entire logic of Christian effort in one line. He is not running to be apprehended; he was apprehended on the Damascus road, seized by a light and a voice while he was travelling in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag. Every step since has been the response of a man already taken.

Get that order wrong and the Christian life becomes unbearable. Running to be caught is exhausting and never finished. Running because you were caught is something else entirely — and it is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him.

“But one thing I do.” Consider who is saying it. A man with a dozen churches on his conscience, a trial pending, letters to write, collections to organise. And he says his life has one thing in it. Not a balanced portfolio of priorities. One.

“Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead.” The picture is a runner in the stadium — and “straining forward” is a vivid compound suggesting the whole body stretched out toward the tape, the way a sprinter’s chest reaches the line ahead of his legs. Note that biblical forgetting is not amnesia; Paul remembers his past perfectly well and has just spent six verses listing it. It means refusing to let it govern. And it cuts both ways, which is the pastoral gold here. The runner must forget his failures — Paul had a genuinely terrible past, blood on his hands, and could have spent his life doing penance in his own head. And he must forget his successes, which is harder and less often preached. A man glancing back at either one is a man losing the race.

“I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call.” The brabeion was the wreath handed down at the games, and the games were a fixture of life in a city like Philippi. But Paul’s prize is not a wreath; it is “the upward call of God in Christ Jesus” — and the herald’s summons calling the victor up to receive it is the same summons that will call him up at the end. The prize is not a thing God gives. It is God calling him home.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let those of us who are mature think this way.” The word is teleioi — and it is the same root as “perfect” in verse 12, where Paul denied being it. He is doing something deliberate and slightly wry. Three verses ago: I am not teleios. Now: let those of us who are teleioi think this way. The apparent contradiction is the lesson. Maturity is not having arrived; maturity is knowing you have not. The mark of a grown-up Christian is precisely the refusal to claim completion, and anyone who thinks he has finished has thereby proved he has not started thinking properly.

Then verse 15b, which is one of the most gracious sentences Paul ever wrote about disagreement: “and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you.”

Consider the restraint. This is an apostle, writing with authority, who has just spent twelve verses on the most important doctrine there is, and who two paragraphs earlier called his opponents dogs. He is perfectly capable of pressing. And on this matter he does not. He does not repeat the argument louder, threaten, or demand immediate agreement. He hands them over to God and expects God to do the work.

The distinction he is making is one every church needs and few manage. On the gospel itself — whether righteousness comes by law or by faith — Paul gives no ground whatever; there the language is dogs and mutilators. On the outworking of the pressing-on life, where sincere Christians see differently, he is patient and confident that the Spirit who teaches will keep teaching. Knowing which question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom. Treat every disagreement as a first-order matter and you will shred a congregation; treat none of them as first-order and you will lose the gospel.

Notice also what he does not say. He does not say the disagreement does not matter, or that both views are equally good. He plainly thinks he is right and expects them to come round — “God will reveal that also to you.” This is patience, not indifference. Paul is confident enough in the truth to let God do the persuading, which is a very different thing from being unsure whether there is anything to persuade anyone of.

And then the floor, in verse 16: “Only let us hold true to what we have attained.” The verb is a marching word — keep in step with, stay in line with. Whatever remains unresolved, walk consistently in the light you already have. It is a wonderfully practical instruction for anyone stuck on a question they cannot settle. You do not have to solve everything before you obey anything. Live up to what you know, and trust God for the rest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Two Ways to Walk, and Where You Are From
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul offers himself as a pattern — and immediately widens it, telling them to keep their eyes on anyone who walks the same way (v.17). Against that he sets people he can hardly write about without weeping: many walk as enemies of the cross of Christ (v.18). Four marks are given, and they descend from the terminus to the root — their end is destruction, their god is their belly, they glory in their shame, and their minds are set on earthly things (v.19).

Then the hinge. But our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we are watching the road for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (v.20) — who will transform the body of our humiliation into the likeness of his body of glory, by the power that enables him to subject all things to himself (v.21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Citizenship, and a Body That Will Be Raised

The noun in verse 20 is politeuma, sister to the verb Paul used at 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. He planted it there; here is the flower. And the picture is not evacuation. A Roman colonia — which is exactly what Philippi was, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil — was not a party of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat. It was Rome made visible on the frontier. Heavenly citizenship does not license withdrawal from the city; it tells you what you are doing there. Note too that Soter and Kyrios were both Caesar’s titles, said in a town full of men who had sworn him an oath.

Verse 21 completes the pattern of the chapter 2 hymn and turns it on us. There Christ took the form of a slave; here the body of our humiliation — the noun is the one behind “he humbled himself” in 2:8 — is conformed to his body of glory. Against the Greek assumption that salvation means the soul escaping the body, Paul insists the body is not the problem and will not be discarded but changed: the same body made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own and still bore the wounds. And the guarantee runs from greater to lesser — the power that will subject all things to him is the power that will be applied to your body.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Join in imitating me” sounds arrogant until you remember what these Christians did not have: no New Testament, no shelf of books, no Christian upbringing, most of them a few years out of paganism. The gospel had to be seen before it could be copied, and it had reached them in a man they had watched flogged in their own marketplace and singing at midnight in their own jail. Note also who says it — the man who five verses earlier said he had not arrived. That is what makes him safe to follow: he is not exhibiting a finished product but the direction of a life.

Now: The searching phrase in verse 19 is the last and quietest: “minds set on earthly things.” It does not describe an act but an orientation — where the mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention. Not what you would name as your priorities; what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. And verse 21 is a word for one reader in particular: the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail. Scripture does not say the body does not matter. It says the body matters so much that God intends to raise it. What you live in now is the body of humiliation. It is not the last word about you.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Join in imitating me” — and the modern reader flinches. Is that not arrogance? It would be, but for three things. First, Paul never means it without the qualifier he makes explicit elsewhere: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1). He is not the destination; he is a signpost, and a signpost points away from itself. Second, remember what these Christians did not have: no New Testament, no shelf of books, no Christian upbringing — most of them only a few years out of paganism. The gospel had to be seen before it could be copied. It reached them not as a set of propositions but in a man they had watched with their own eyes — flogged in their own city, and singing hymns at midnight in the cell (Acts 16:22–25).

Third, look who is saying it. Five verses earlier this same man wrote that he had not obtained it and was not yet perfect. The one who says “imitate me” is the one who has just said he has not arrived — and that is exactly what makes him safe to follow. He is not displaying a finished product; he is showing you the direction of a life.

Notice, too, how quickly he widens it: “keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us.” Not Paul only. Any life bent that way will do. Somewhere in your own congregation there is a quiet old saint worth watching more closely than you have.

Then the contrast, and Paul’s composure breaks: “many… walk as enemies of the cross of Christ.” He says he tells them this “even with tears.” That is the tone to hold on to. He is not sneering at these people or enjoying the denunciation. He is weeping while he writes, which is the only posture from which anyone should ever describe another person’s ruin.

Who are they? Paul does not say, and the description fits more than one group. What he gives is not a doctrinal profile but a way of walking — which is the point. These are enemies of the cross practically, not theoretically. The cross is the pattern of chapter 2: self-emptying, obedience, the interests of others. A life organised around self-indulgence contradicts that pattern whatever it professes on a Sunday.

Four marks are given, and they descend. “Their end is destruction” — the terminus, named first, because Paul wants the trajectory visible before the symptoms. “Their god is their belly” — appetite in the place of worship; whatever in you says I want has been enthroned, and it is a god that must be fed daily and never says thank you. “They glory in their shame” — the boast has been inverted; the very things that should have caused them to hide are the things they advertise. And the root of all of it: “with minds set on earthly things.”

That last phrase is the diagnosis, and it is quieter than the others — which makes it the more searching. It does not describe an act but an orientation: where the mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention. Not what you would say your priorities are. What you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. That is the thing Paul is weeping over, and it is far more ordinary than the phrase “enemies of the cross” leads us to expect.

verseByVerse.quote: But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But.” The hinge of the chapter. Against minds set on earthly things, Paul sets a single fact about where his readers actually belong.

“Our citizenship is in heaven.” The noun is politeuma, and it is the sister of the verb Paul used back in 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. He planted the seed there; here is the flower. A politeuma was a body of citizens resident in a foreign place, holding the rights and duties of a homeland they might never have seen.

And every reader in Philippi lived inside that arrangement. Philippi was a Roman colonia, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil. Its people wore Roman dress, used Roman law, and minted Latin coins in a Greek province, and they were intensely proud of it — the charge against Paul in that very city had been that he was disturbing customs “not lawful for us as Romans to accept” (Acts 16:21). Paul takes the proudest fact about their city and tells them it is a parable of something truer: you already know what it is to live in one place and belong to another. Now transpose it. Your capital is not Rome.

Which corrects the usual misreading of this verse. “Citizenship in heaven” is not a promise of evacuation and it is not permission to disengage. A Roman colony was not a group of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat. It was Rome’s presence on the frontier, established precisely so that the distant capital would be visible where it otherwise was not. Paul is not telling them to withdraw from Philippi. He is telling them what they are doing there.

“And from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.” The verb is a strong compound — to await eagerly, expectantly. And the two titles are chosen with care. Soter, saviour, and Kyrios, lord, were both claimed by Caesar; the emperor was routinely styled saviour of the world. In a colony full of retired soldiers who had sworn an oath to him, Paul says quietly that the Saviour and Lord is someone else, and he is the one we are watching the road for. A colony always expects a visit from its king. The question this verse asks is not whether you believe he is coming, but whether anything in the way you live this week would only make sense if he were.

verseByVerse.quote: who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter’s last great sentence, and it takes the hymn of chapter 2 and turns it on us. There, Christ was transformed — from the form of God to the form of a slave, and then exalted. Here, we are: he “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body.” The verb behind “to be like” is built on morphe again, the same root as “the form of God” in 2:6 and “becoming like him in his death” in verse 10. The pattern completes: he took our form so that we might take his.

“Our lowly body” is literally the body of our humiliation — and the word is the noun behind “he humbled himself” in 2:8. Paul is not sneering at the body. He is naming what everyone over forty already knows: these bodies are in a humiliated condition. They tire, thicken, fail, forget, and are finally laid in the ground. Anyone who has watched a strong parent become unable to manage a staircase knows exactly what phrase Paul has chosen, and knows he has not exaggerated.

And against that, the promise is not escape from the body but its transformation. This matters, and the church has often got it wrong. The Greek world around Philippi mostly held that salvation meant the soul getting free of the body, which was the problem. Paul says the body is not the problem and will not be discarded; it will be changed. The same body, made glorious — as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own, still bearing the wounds, and yet transfigured. Whatever is buried is what is raised (1 Cor 15:42–44).

Then the guarantee, and Paul does not leave the promise hanging on sentiment: “by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.” The argument is from the greater to the lesser. The energy that will one day bring the entire created order under Christ’s feet — every hostile power, death included — is the energy that will be applied to your body. If he can do the first, the second is not going to strain him.

Set that beside where the chapter began. Paul opened by throwing his pedigree out with the kitchen refuse and closed by promising that the humiliated body will be made like the body of glory. In between he told them not to set their minds on earthly things. This is why. Not because earthly things are unreal, but because they are not where the story is going.

And it is a word for a particular reader — the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail. The New Testament does not tell you the body does not matter. It tells you the body matters so much that God intends to raise it. What you are living in now is the body of humiliation; it is not the last word about you, and the one who will have the last word has the power to subject all things to himself.

4.title: The Peace That Passes Understanding: Rejoice, Pray, and Be Content
4.overview:
The final chapter of Philippians gathers the letter’s dominant notes into a sustained chord of joy, peace, and contentment. It begins with an affectionate address to the church as Paul’s “joy and crown” and moves immediately to a specific pastoral intervention: Euodia and Syntyche, two women who have laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel, are in conflict, and Paul appeals directly for their reconciliation. The specificity is characteristic of Paul: the gospel always comes to particular people in particular situations, not to an abstract community in a general condition.

The chapter’s great passage (vv. 4–7) is one of the most quoted in Paul’s letters: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice.” The repetition is not rhetorical padding; it is the recognition that the command requires emphasis because the natural response to difficulty is not joy. The peace of God that passes understanding is not achieved by following the right steps; it is given by the God of peace to those who bring everything to him in prayer with thanksgiving. The movement is from anxiety to prayer to peace — not from anxiety to resolved circumstances to peace.

The “whatever is true” list of verse 8 is Paul’s most explicit engagement with the Graeco-Roman virtue tradition, commandeering its language for the gospel’s purposes: whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, commendable — think about these things. The mind shaped by these realities is the mind that can sustain the peace God gives. And the great biographical testimony of verses 10–13 — the secret of contentment, learned in plenty and in need, in abundance and in want — is Paul’s autobiography of grace applied to circumstance: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” Not the triumphalist claim that Christ will give you whatever you want, but the humble confession that Christ’s strength is sufficient for whatever he calls you to endure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens the chapter with one of the warmest addresses in the New Testament: the Philippians are his “brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown.” The “crown” (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games — the prize of a race well run. The Philippians are Paul’s eschatological prize, the evidence that his running was not in vain (3:14). This warmth immediately provides the context for the difficult pastoral word that follows: “I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord.”

The appeal for reconciliation is remarkable for what Paul does and does not say. He does not take sides; he does not adjudicate who is right. He appeals to each by name, separately (“I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche”), and he does so “in the Lord” — the ground of their unity is not their agreement on the disputed point but their shared life in Christ. He then enlists a third party to help; and he reminds everyone that these women “have laboured side by side with me in the gospel.” Their conflict does not erase their history or their contribution; it is a present grief that does not define them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reconciliation in the Lord and the Foundation of Christian Unity

The appeal to Euodia and Syntyche illustrates the Reformed understanding of the ground of Christian unity: it is not agreement on every point but the shared life in Christ, the common Lord, the one Spirit. Unity “in the Lord” is possible even before the dispute is resolved because it rests on something more fundamental than the dispute. The community that grounds its unity in doctrinal consensus or personal agreement will be perpetually fractured; the community that grounds its unity in Christ will be able to sustain the friction of genuine disagreement without breaking.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Euodia and Syntyche were genuine gospel workers who had served Paul faithfully. Their conflict was real and damaging enough that Paul addresses it publicly, from prison, across the distance. Even the most faithful workers in the gospel can be in conflict; the question is whether the gospel’s resources will be brought to bear on the conflict. Now: Every congregation has its Euodias and Syntyches — genuine believers in genuine conflict. The pastoral response Paul models is not avoidance (he names them) and not adjudication (he takes no side) but appeal to the Lord in whom they are both found, and the enlistment of the community’s help in the work of reconciliation.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved. I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Stand firm thus in the Lord” — the “thus” gathers up all of chapters 1–3: stand firm in the citizenship of heaven (3:20), in the gospel (1:27), in the Christ who holds you fast (3:12). “Agree in the Lord” (to auto phronein en kyriō) — the same mind in the Lord, the mind of Christ (2:5). The agreement Paul seeks is not forced conformity but the genuine meeting of minds in Christ that is possible when both parties are genuinely submitted to him. “Whose names are in the book of life” — an extraordinary affirmation for two women in conflict: their conflict does not define them; their election does. They are in the book of life, and that is the truth that must govern how the community sees and treats them through the difficulty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Rejoice, Pray, and Think on These Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The four commands of verses 4–7 are among the most practically transformative in the New Testament: rejoice in the Lord always; let your reasonableness be known to everyone; do not be anxious about anything; in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. The sequence is not coincidental. Rejoicing in the Lord is the foundation: the God in whom you rejoice is the ground of everything else. The reasonableness (epieikeia — gentleness, graciousness, forbearance) that others see in you flows from the security of those who know the Lord is near. And prayer displaces anxiety not by resolving the circumstances that cause it but by redirecting the energy of worry toward God.

The peace of God “which surpasses all understanding” is the result, not of the resolution of problems, but of the act of bringing them to God. It is a peace that logic cannot produce and cannot explain — a peace that “guards” (the military metaphor: stands sentinel over) the heart and mind in Christ Jesus. Following this, verse 8’s list of things to think on is not a self-help positive-thinking program; it is the Christian mind actively orienting itself toward what is genuinely good, true, and beautiful — the realities that reflect God’s own character — as the content of its meditation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer, Peace, and the Guarding of the Heart

Philippians 4:6–7 is the New Testament’s most direct treatment of anxiety and its remedy. The remedy is not improved circumstances, not cognitive reframing, not better stress management — it is prayer. The transfer of the thing that causes anxiety from the heart’s grip to God’s hands — with thanksgiving, not resignation — is what produces the peace that surpasses understanding. Reformed spirituality has always insisted that prayer is not an additional spiritual technique but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator, the child before the Father, the dependent before the one on whom all dependence rests.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philippians had real causes for anxiety: Paul in prison, their own community in conflict, external opposition, the uncertainty of the future. The peace Paul prescribes is not the peace of resolved circumstances but the peace of the surrendered heart. They can experience it now, in the middle of the unresolved circumstances, because the peace depends not on what has changed but on who holds what has not. Now: The anxious Christian — worried about health, finances, relationships, the future — is invited not to stop worrying (an exercise of pure willpower that reliably fails) but to pray: to bring the thing to God, specifically, with thanksgiving, and to leave it there. The peace is God’s gift to those who do this; it cannot be manufactured by those who do not.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Let your reasonableness be known to everyone. The Lord is at hand; do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Rejoice in the Lord always” — the qualifier “in the Lord” is the key that makes “always” possible. Joy based on circumstances cannot be always; joy rooted in the unchanging Lord can be. “The Lord is at hand” — both near in presence (he is with you) and near in time (his return is certain). Both senses fuel the reasonableness and the freedom from anxiety: the Lord who is present holds what you cannot, and the Lord who is coming will resolve what you cannot. “With thanksgiving” — the element that transforms prayer from negotiation with God into communion with God. Thanksgiving acknowledges that the one you are petitioning is already good, already faithful, already working — so the petition is made from a posture of trust rather than demand. The peace that “guards” (phrourēsei, the garrison of soldiers keeping watch) is not a feeling to be cultivated but a gift to be received.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me — practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The virtue-list of verse 8 is Paul at his most culturally engaged: the language of “honourable,” “just,” “commendable,” and “excellent” was the vocabulary of Graeco-Roman moral philosophy, commandeered for the gospel’s purposes. Paul is not blessing a self-sufficient morality that has no need of God; he is affirming that wherever genuine goodness, truth, beauty, and justice appear in human culture, they are reflections of the God in whose image humanity was made, and they are worth dwelling on. The mind shaped by these realities is the mind capable of sustaining the peace God gives. Then verse 9 turns from thinking to doing, and gathers four verbs: what you have “learned and received” — the teaching handed on to them, the apostolic deposit — and what you have “heard and seen in me” — that same teaching embodied in a life they had watched. Doctrine and demonstration; the message and the man. It is the point he pressed at 3:17, and it is why he could press it: a gospel that has only been heard is half-delivered. And then the verb that governs them all — “practice these things.” Not admire them, not discuss them, not merely believe them. Do them. “The God of peace will be with you” — not merely the peace of God (v. 7) but the God of peace himself: his presence, not merely his gift, is the prize of the obedient and thoughtful life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter’s final movement is Paul’s letter of thanks for the Philippians’ financial gift — and it is the most theologically profound thank-you letter ever written. He rejoices in their gift, not because he was in desperate need (he has learned to be content in any circumstance) but because it is evidence of their faithfulness and a fragrant offering to God. The thanks come last in the letter because Paul wanted to establish first that his joy was not dependent on their gift; it came from the Lord who is always near.

The claim of verse 11 — “I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content” — is one of the most remarkable statements in the New Testament. Contentment, Paul says, is not a natural temperament or a philosophical disposition; it is something learned. And the curriculum is the experience of both extremes: “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound.” The Stoics sought contentment through indifference to circumstances; Paul seeks it through the One who is Lord over all circumstances. The difference is everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contentment as the Fruit of Christ-Sufficiency

The Reformed tradition has always understood contentment as a spiritual discipline rooted in theological conviction: God is sovereign, his purposes are good, his provision is sufficient, and nothing that comes to the believer falls outside his governance. The Westminster Larger Catechism lists “holy contentment” as a duty required by the tenth commandment, and its opposite — “inordinate desire for, or love of, the world and the things thereof” — as its violation. Contentment is not passive acceptance of all circumstances as equally desirable; it is the active trust that the God who governs all circumstances is sufficient for all of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had experienced literal hunger, literal abundance, literal poverty, literal plenty. His contentment was not philosophical; it was forged in specific, concrete experiences of both having and not having. The secret he had learned — Christ’s strengthening in every circumstance — was earned through the full range of human extremity. Now: The “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” has been disastrously misread as a promise that Christ will help you achieve your ambitions. In context, it means precisely the opposite: Christ’s strength is sufficient to enable you to be content when you have nothing, to maintain your integrity when you have everything, to press on when the circumstances are against you. It is the promise of sufficiency, not of triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoiced in the Lord greatly that now at length you have revived your concern for me… Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I have learned” — contentment is a learned skill, acquired through practice, not a gift delivered complete at conversion. The curriculum is the full range of experience: “brought low” and “abound,” “hungry” and “plenty.” The “secret” of contentment — Paul uses the language of being initiated into a mystery — is Christ himself: “through him who strengthens me.” The strengthening is continuous and personal, an ongoing empowerment available in every circumstance. Christ is the source of the capacity to face whatever comes — low or high, empty or full, free or chained. “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” is not a promise of athletic success; it is the testimony of a man who has been in prison and found it enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet it was kind of you to share my trouble. And you Philippians yourselves know that in the beginning of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving except you only… Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that increases to your credit. I have received full payment, and more. I am well supplied… And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The history of the partnership is movingly specific: “in the beginning of the gospel, when I left Macedonia.” They had been with him from the start, and they alone among the churches had maintained the financial partnership throughout. The fruit Paul seeks is not for himself (“not that I seek the gift”) but for them — the spiritual credit that accrues to those who invest in the gospel’s advance. Their gift is a “fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” — the language of temple worship applied to the financial support of gospel ministry: their money is their worship. The promise of verse 19 — “my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” — is the theological reciprocal of their generosity: those who give from God’s riches will find that God supplies from his riches. The God who is infinitely rich in glory is also infinitely generous toward those who trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Those of Caesar’s household” — the household staff and slaves of the Roman emperor, who apparently included some who had come to faith through Paul’s imprisonment ministry (1:13). The gospel, which had arrived in Philippi at a riverside prayer meeting, had now penetrated the household of the most powerful man in the world. The irony is exquisite: the prisoner’s chains had opened doors the free apostle could never have entered. The final word is as simple as the letter’s first: grace. “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” Grace is the beginning and the end, the ground on which the entire letter stands, the one word that summarizes everything Paul has written: the free, unmerited, inexhaustible gift of God in Jesus Christ, sufficient for every circumstance, available to every need, the only ground on which any person, in any prison, in any city, at any moment, can stand.
